### Bounded Sets (Real Numbers)

:::{.definition data-title="Bounded Real Sets"}

A set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ is **bounded from above** if there exists
$M \in \mathbb{R}$, called an **upper bound** of $A$, such that $x \leq M$ for
all $x \in A$. Similarly, $A$ is **bounded from below** if there exists
$m \in \mathbb{R}$, called a **lower bound** of $A$, such that $x \geq m$ for
all $x \in A$. A set $A$ is **bounded** if it is bounded both from above and
below, equivalently if $A \subset [m,M]$ for some $m,M\in\mathbb{R}$.

:::

### Supremum & Infimum (Real Numbers)

The **supremum** and **infimum** are key concepts for defining
[[completeness|completeness]]. In real analysis, we can use the
[[order|ordering properties]] of $\mathbb{R}$ to define the supremum and
infimum of a set of real numbers.  

:::{.definition data-title="Supremum & Infimum"}

The set of real numbers $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ has an upper bound
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $M \leq M'$ for every upper bound $M'$ of $A$,
then $M$ is the **least upper bound** or **supremum** of $A$, denoted
$$
M=\sup{A}.
$$
Similarly, if $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ has a lower bound $m \in \mathbb{R}$ such
that $m\geq m'$ for every lower bound $m'$ of $A$, then $m$ is the **greatest
lower bound** or **infimum** of $A$, denoted
$$
m=\inf{A}.
$$

:::

If $A=\{ x_{i}:i \in I \}$ is an indexed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ we write
$$
\sup{A}=\sup_{i \in I}{x_{i}},\quad \quad \inf{A}=\inf_{i \in I}{x_{i}}.
$$
Note that if $M,m \in A$ then the supremum $M$ and infimum $m$ are equivalent
to the maximum and minimum respectively. The key point is that the supremum and
infimum need not belong to the set $A$.

:::{.definition}

If a set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ is not bounded from above, then
$\sup_{}{A}= \infty$ and if $A$ is not bounded from below then
$\inf_{}{A}=-\infty$.

:::

### Supremum & Infimum Properties

:::{.theorem}

If $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ then $M = \sup_{}{A}$ if and only if:
1. $M$ is an upper bound of $A$;
2. $\forall M'<M,~\exists x \in A~:~x>M'$.

Similarly, $m = \inf_{}{A}$ if and only if:
1. $m$ is a lower bound of $A$; and
2. $\forall m'>m,~\exists x \in A~:~x<m'$.

:::

We frequently use this proposition as follows:

1. If $M$ is an upper bound of $A$; then $\sup_{}{A}\leq M$.
2. If you $A$ is nonempty and bounded from above, then for every
   $\varepsilon>0,~\exists x \in A~s.t. x>\sup_{}{A}-\varepsilon$.

### Supremum & Infimum of Extended Real Sequences

Consider an extended real sequence
$\{ x_{n} \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}\cup \{ \pm \infty \}$.
A number $u \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is an **upper bound** of the sequence if
$x_{n}\leq u$ for all $n$, and the sequence is **bounded above**. Similarly,
$l \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is a **lower bound** if $x_{n}\geq l$ for all $n$,
and the sequence is **bounded below**. A sequence is **bounded** if it is both
bounded above and below.

:::{.definition data-title="Supremum & Infimum of a Sequence"}

The **supremum** $\sup_{n}{x_{n}}$ is the unique **least upper bound** of the
sequence: it is an upper bound, and $\sup_{n}x_{n}\leq u$ for every upper bound
$u$. The **infimum** $\inf_{n}{x_{n}}$ is the unique **greatest lower bound**:
it is a lower bound, and $\inf_{n}x_{n}\geq l$ for every lower bound $l$.

:::

These are fundamental definitions in [[measure-theory-notes]] and
[[real-analysis]], where they form the basis for defining limits, continuity and
integrals, and in particular [[limsup-liminf]].

:::{.theorem data-title="Infimum and Supremum Inequality"}

For an extended real sequence $\{ x_{n} \}$,
$$
\inf_{n}{x_{n}}\leq x_{k}\leq \sup_{n}{x_{n}}\quad\text{for all }k.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
The infimum is a lower bound and the supremum is an upper bound, so
$\inf_nx_n\leq x_k\leq\sup_nx_n$ for each $k$ by definition.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Order Preservation"}

If $x_{n}\leq y_{n}$ for all $n$ then
$$
\inf_{n}{x_{n}}\leq \inf_{n}{y_{n}},\qquad \sup_{n}{x_{n}}\leq \sup_{n}{y_{n}}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
For every $n$, $x_n\leq y_n\leq\sup_ky_k$, so $\sup_ky_k$ is an upper bound of
$\{x_n\}$ and hence $\sup_nx_n\leq\sup_ky_k$. Similarly
$\inf_kx_k\leq x_n\leq y_n$ for every $n$, so $\inf_kx_k$ is a lower bound of
$\{y_n\}$ and hence $\inf_kx_k\leq\inf_ny_n$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Inequalities of Sums"}

For sequences $\{ x_{n} \},\{ y_{n} \}$ (with no $\infty-\infty$),
$$
\sup_{n}(x_{n}+y_{n})\leq \sup_{n}{x_{n}}+\sup_{n}{y_{n}},\qquad
\inf_{n}{(x_{n}+y_{n})}\geq \inf_{n}{x_{n}}+\inf_{n}{y_{n}}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
For every $n$, $x_n+y_n\leq\sup_kx_k+\sup_ky_k$, so the right-hand side is an
upper bound of $\{x_n+y_n\}$ and hence dominates its supremum. The infimum
statement is analogous. (We cannot argue with an index $m$ attaining the
supremum, as the supremum need not be attained.)
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Inequalities of Products"}

For **nonnegative** sequences $\{ x_{n} \}, \{ y_{n} \}$,
$$
\sup_{n}{(x_{n}y_{n})}\leq \sup_{n}{x_{n}}\cdot \sup_{n}{y_{n}},\qquad
\inf_{n}{(x_{n}y_{n})}\geq \inf_{n}{x_{n}}\cdot \inf_{n}{y_{n}}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
As for sums, using $0\leq x_n\leq\sup_kx_k$ and $0\leq y_n\leq\sup_ky_k$ to bound
$x_ny_n$, and similarly with the infima. Nonnegativity is needed: for $x_n=y_n=-n$ we have
$\sup x_n=\sup y_n=-1$, but $\sup_n x_ny_n=\sup_n n^2=+\infty>1$.
:::
